cues.text: A language exchange is a trade: you give something, and you get something back.
You help someone with your language, and they help you with theirs.
For example, you speak Japanese and want to practise English.
So you look for an English speaker who wants to practise Japanese.
Everyone is a teacher and a student at the same time.
In this lesson, you visit the Dutch Language Café in The Hague.
The Hague is a city in the Netherlands.
Every Thursday at 19:30, its language exchange starts.
Every visitor gets a language sticker.
You write your languages on it and wear it on your shirt.
You write the languages you speak, and your native language is one of them.
Your native language is the first language you learned as a child.
You also write the languages you want to practise.
Why a sticker?
The room is full of strangers, people you do not know.
With one look at a sticker, you know who can help you.
A sticker also gives you your first question.
Do you see Spanish on someone's sticker?
Then ask: I see you study Spanish.
Why?
At 20:00, the speed exchange starts.
You talk with one person for 3 minutes.
Then you move to the next person.
You and your partner take turns choosing the language.
First one of you chooses, then the other.
This way, both people practise.
Why only 3 minutes?
In a short time, you meet many new people.
You also find the people you want to talk to again.
At 20:30, everyone sits down at language tables.
For example, there is an English table and a Spanish table.
At each table, people talk or play games in one language.
At 21:10, you can change tables and try a new language.
At the Dutch Language Café, a Thursday ticket costs €11.
The ticket includes the snacks and the games: they are in the price.
The snacks are popcorn, crisps and nuts.
You can eat some at your table for free.
But drinks are not included.
You buy them at the bar from the bartender.
The bartender is the person who works behind the bar.
You buy food there too.
On the menu, you see a funny name: koffie verkeerd.
In English, it means wrong coffee.
Why wrong?
A normal Dutch coffee has only a little milk.
Koffie verkeerd has a lot of warm milk, often more than the coffee.
So it is the wrong way around.
It costs €4.00.
If you are hungry, try an empanada.
An empanada is small and baked, with food inside.
Here, you choose cheese, meat or spinach inside.
One empanada costs €6.50.
A bar is loud, and a menu has new words.
When you do not understand, do not just say yes.
Ask: Sorry, can you say that again?
Or ask about the new word: What does spinach mean?
At a language café, everyone is a student, so questions are normal.
A short answer helps you get the right drink and the right food.
In the Netherlands, people shake hands when they meet someone new.
At the same time, they say their name, often only the first name.
Hi!
I'm Sanne.
In Japan, many people bow, or bend forward, and say their family name.
The name is important.
The Leiden International Centre helps people who move to the Netherlands.
It says that a hello without your name is rude, or not polite.
Why?
Your name tells people who you are.
It also tells them what to call you all evening.
So when you hear a new name, say your name too.
Then say: Nice to meet you.
At a first meeting, do not ask: How are you?
For many Dutch people, it is a real question, not just a hello.
They ask it when they really want to know the answer.
So they usually ask people they already know.
At a first meeting, just say hello and your name.
Save How are you?
for next Thursday, when you meet again.
In a 3-minute speed exchange, you do not have much time.
So say three things: your name, your city and why you study the language.
Daan says: Hi!
I'm Daan.
I live in The Hague.
I study Japanese because I'm going to Tokyo in April.
The last part is the most useful.
It gives the other person a question.
For example: What do you want to see in Tokyo?
When you finish, ask back: What about you?
The best tool for a long conversation is the follow-up question.
A follow-up question is a question about what the other person just said.
Lucía says: I moved here from Valencia.
A new question jumps to a new idea: Do you like football?
A follow-up question stays with her idea: Why did you move here?
She answers: For work.
I work at a hotel.
Now you take one part of her answer.
Then you ask again: What do you do at the hotel?
Each answer gives you the next question.
In 2017, scientists at Harvard University studied conversations between strangers.
People who asked more questions were liked more by their partners.
Follow-up questions worked best.
Why?
A follow-up question shows that you are really listening.
But there is one problem.
If you never talk about yourself, people may think you are hiding something.
A good conversation goes both ways.
React to what you hear, for example: Really?
Me too!
Or say: That sounds fun!
Then tell something about yourself, and ask back.
At 21:30, the exchange ends.
Do not just walk away: the other person gave you their time.
Say: It was nice to talk to you.
Do you want to keep in touch, or talk again later?
Ask for WhatsApp.
In the Netherlands, WhatsApp is by far the most used app for messages.
Almost every phone there has it.
So almost everyone you meet can say yes.
The exchange is every Thursday, so you can also say: See you next Thursday!
